name: BLAKE3
baseline: OpenSSL SHA-256, OpenSSL SHA3-256, BLAKE2b, BLAKE2s
workload: Hashing a 16 KiB buffer, single-threaded, via `cargo bench '16384$'`, comparing BLAKE3 against OpenSSL-backed MD5/SHA-1/SHA-2/SHA-3 and the blake2b_simd/blake2s_simd crates
claimed_speedup: 6866 MB/s for BLAKE3 vs 484 MB/s OpenSSL SHA-256 (~14.2x), 394 MB/s OpenSSL SHA3-256 (~17.4x), 1312 MB/s BLAKE2b (~5.2x), 876 MB/s BLAKE2s (~7.8x) (derived from page data)
compiler_and_flags: cargo bench (Rust release build); RUSTFLAGS="-C target-cpu=native" was additionally set for the BLAKE2b/BLAKE2s crates only, to enable AVX-512 rotations; BLAKE3 and OpenSSL used default flags
hardware: AWS c5.metal instance, Intel Cascade Lake-SP 8275CL
tradeoffs: Different digest from SHA-2/SHA-3/BLAKE2 (not a bit-compatible drop-in); Merkle-tree construction parallelizes across threads and SIMD lanes; official optimized implementations in Rust and C; explicitly not recommended for password hashing.
caveats: Benchmark is 16 KiB inputs only; giving the BLAKE2 crates target-cpu=native while leaving BLAKE3/OpenSSL at default flags could modestly favor BLAKE2's baseline rather than disadvantage it, so the reported BLAKE3 margin is if anything conservative; hardware is a 2019-era Cascade Lake part.
found_via: gh search + direct open of BLAKE3-team/BLAKE3 README, cross-checked against linked BLAKE3-specs/benchmarks/bar_chart.py

name: KangarooTwelve (K12, via XKCP)
workload: Long-message XOF/hash throughput (cycles/byte) on a single core, using the 12-round Keccak-p permutation with SIMD/parallel tree hashing
claimed_speedup: KT128 at <1.5 cycles/byte on Haswell/Skylake, 0.51 cycles/byte on SkylakeX/Cascade Lake, and 0.75 cycles/byte on Apple A14/M1 (using ARMv8-A SHA-3 instructions); ~2x speedup over SHAKE128 for short messages and low-end platforms
hardware: Intel Haswell, Skylake, SkylakeX, Cascade Lake; Apple A14/M1
license: CC0-1.0 (inherited from parent XKCP project; this trimmed repo ships no separate LICENSE file, and a few files carry other permissive third-party licenses per XKCP/XKCP's LICENSE)
stars_or_usage: 53 stars (this trimmed extraction); parent XKCP/XKCP has 664 stars and is the Keccak team's reference codebase behind FIPS 202/SP 800-185/RFC 9861
tradeoffs: Different algorithm from SHA-3/SHAKE (12 rounds instead of 24, tree-hash Sakura encoding) so not a bit-compatible drop-in; officially specified in RFC 9861 and an ACNS paper (design basis: IACR ePrint 2016/770).
caveats: Cycles/byte figures are vendor/project-reported in the README, not tied to a documented compiler invocation or flags; underlying design is peer-reviewed (ACNS, IACR ePrint 2016/770) but the specific numbers quoted here come from the project's own docs, not that paper's benchmark harness.
found_via: gh search repos "KangarooTwelve"; opened XKCP/K12 README and cross-checked design claims against IACR ePrint 2016/770 ("KangarooTwelve: fast hashing based on Keccak-p")

name: j-lanes tree hashing mode and j-lanes SHA-256 (Gueron)
workload: SHA-256 hashing of single messages ranging 2KB-132KB, using a 4-lanes SIMD tree-hashing mode (j=4) on AVX, versus standard serial SHA-256
claimed_speedup: ~2x to ~2.53x faster than OpenSSL 1.0.1c; 1.5x-1.97x faster than the fastest publicly available SHA-256 implementation known to the authors; also faster than tree-mode BLAKE and Keccak (SHA-3 finalists)
hardware: 3rd Generation Intel Core processor (Ivy Bridge, AVX)
tradeoffs: Requires restructuring hashing into a tree mode (message split into j independent SIMD lanes, then combined), which changes the digest unless both hasher and verifier use the same mode; needs AVX; author was an Intel researcher and later pushed related multi-buffer techniques toward OpenSSL/ISA-L.
caveats: IACR ePrint preprint; no compiler or compile flags stated; no public benchmark code linked from the paper; hardware and OpenSSL version (2012-era Ivy Bridge, OpenSSL 1.0.1c) are now over a decade old, so absolute margins on modern OpenSSL (with its own AVX2/SHA-NI paths) are likely smaller.
found_via: IACR ePrint site search "SHA-256 SIMD faster" -> https://eprint.iacr.org/2012/476, opened and read PDF via curl+pdftotext

name: Simultaneous hashing of multiple messages / S-HASH (Gueron & Krasnov)
workload: 4-buffer parallel (multi-buffer) SHA-256 hashing of multiple independent messages, measured from CPU cache/memory and from disk
claimed_speedup: 3.42x faster than OpenSSL 1.0.1 hashing from cache/memory (5.2 cycles/byte); ~3x faster than OpenSSL 1.0.1 hashing from disk (6.73 cycles/byte); 2.25x faster than the contemporary n-SMS method
tradeoffs: Only pays off when multiple independent messages/buffers can be hashed concurrently (e.g. boot-time integrity checks, multi-stream server workloads); unlike j-lanes (2012/476), gives no benefit for a single serial message.
caveats: IACR ePrint preprint; no compiler/flags stated; 2012-era hardware and OpenSSL 1.0.1; paper mentions the technique was proposed as an OpenSSL patch (RT ticket 2784) but does not confirm it was merged.
found_via: IACR ePrint site search "SHA-256 SIMD faster" -> https://eprint.iacr.org/2012/371, opened and read PDF via curl+pdftotext

name: Intel ISA-L Crypto (multi-buffer SHA)
workload: Multi-buffer hashing: running several independent SHA jobs together on one core via SIMD lane interleaving ("Multi-Hash"), versus single-buffer serial SHA-256 on the same core
claimed_speedup: Over 2x faster than 'the best known SHA-256 single buffer implementations', reaching ~5 cycles/byte hashing a 1MB buffer on one core of an Intel Core i7-2600 (per the project's own linked Multi-Hash white paper)
hardware: Intel Core i7-2600 (Sandy Bridge) with Hyper-Threading
tradeoffs: Only accelerates throughput when multiple independent buffers can be scheduled concurrently; needs application-level batching (not a transparent single-call speedup); requires NASM/gas for the hand-written SIMD kernels.
caveats: The 2x number comes from a 2012 Intel white paper describing the general Multi-Hash technique, predating this specific repo's current AVX2/AVX-512 kernels (current numbers are undocumented in-repo, likely better but unverified); the whitepaper says 'best known SHA-256 single buffer implementations' rather than naming OpenSSL explicitly; capped at tier C for the outdated, indirect sourcing.
found_via: Followed from the j-lanes/S-HASH multi-buffer literature (2012/476, 2012/371) to intel/isa-l_crypto, which implements the same multi-buffer technique; read README and linked wiki white paper via curl+pdftotext

name: sha256-simd (minio)
workload: SHA256 hashing of >1MB buffers, single core, comparing the package's own AVX2, Intel SHA Extensions, and AVX512 code paths against each other and against plain Go crypto/sha256
claimed_speedup: AVX512 measured at 3498 MB/s vs 448 MB/s for the AVX2 path (~7.8x) on a 3.0GHz Xeon Platinum 8124M; SHA Extensions measured at 1975 MB/s vs 514 MB/s AVX2 (~3.84x) on Celeron J3455/Ryzen 7 2700X hardware
hardware: 3.0 GHz Intel Xeon Platinum 8124M; Intel Celeron J3455; AMD Ryzen 7 2700X; 1.2GHz ARM Cortex-A53 (Pine64)
stars_or_usage: 1.0k stars; used in the MinIO object storage server for multipart-upload integrity checks
tradeoffs: AVX512 mode requires explicit multi-buffer scheduling (Avx512Server/channels) and only pays off with many concurrent ~5MB-sized SHA256 calls; no benefit for small or single messages; Go-only, not callable from C++.
caveats: Benchmarks compare the package's own code paths against each other and against Go's own crypto/sha256, not against OpenSSL directly, so baseline_in_list is false here; no commits since Feb 2023 (~3.5 years), flagged abandoned.
found_via: gh search repos "SIMD SHA-256"; opened minio/sha256-simd README
